schema:
# GENERATED — the app's own tables. The builder writes this file whole at plan time.
# NO export directive on any table (rule 18): every rule this app enforces is a row rule in
# resources/, and an exported table is a REST route around all of them. `@indexed` on anything a
# resource sorts or filters by (rule 6) — an unindexed search returns empty, silently.
# Short-lived tokens live on @table(expiration:) tables keyed by the token HASH (rule 10).
#
# The sign-in kit brings User, MagicLink, EmailLog and EmailSuppression in schema.sign-in.graphql,
# and the payments kit brings StripeEvent in schema.payments.graphql. Never declare those here: a
# table declared in two files is not merged, it is replaced.
#
# TIMESTAMPS HARPER OWNS. A field carrying @createdTime or @updatedTime is ASSIGNED BY HARPER, in
# epoch milliseconds, which is why each one below is typed Long. Application code must never put a
# value for such a field in a record it writes — not a fresh ISO string, and not the value it read
# back off the stored row a moment earlier. Every field so marked is listed again in CLAUDE.md §8
# with the rule, because this is the whole of a defect that made every admin save answer 400.

# ── template-owned (additive changes only) ───────────────────────────────────

# One row per scheduled run (resources/Scheduler.js). The template's only table: the scheduler is part
# of the bare core and records what it ran. This app writes one row per nightly retention sweep, with
# a deterministic id (clear-personal-details:YYYY-MM-DD) so a repeated tick claims the same row.
type LoopRun @table {
  id: ID @primaryKey
  loop: String @indexed
  startedAt: String @indexed
  finishedAt: String
  outcome: String @indexed
  notes: String
  triggeredBy: String
  node: String
}

# ── app-owned (the builder writes below this line) ───────────────────────────

# One item on the shop's menu. Prices are whole cents, never floats.
# createdAt and updatedAt are Harper's: never written by resources/MenuAdminApi.js (see the header).
# photoUpdatedAt is the app's own plain string: null means this item has no photo, and a non-null
# value is the cache-buster the public menu appends to the photo URL. Not indexed: nothing filters
# or sorts by it — the menu reads it off rows it already has.
type MenuItem @table {
  id: ID @primaryKey
  name: String @indexed
  description: String
  priceCents: Int
  category: String @indexed
  available: Boolean @indexed
  sortOrder: Int @indexed
  photoUpdatedAt: String
  createdAt: Long @createdTime
  updatedAt: Long @updatedTime
}

# One menu item's photo, id = the MenuItem id, so an item has at most one photo and replacing it is
# a put on the same key. A separate table on purpose: the bytes never ride along on a menu listing.
# No managed timestamp here — uploadedAt is a plain string the app writes, so a replace that
# restates the row cannot hit the 400 described in CLAUDE.md §8.
type MenuItemPhoto @table {
  id: ID @primaryKey
  contentType: String
  byteSize: Int
  data: Blob
  uploadedAt: String
}

# One customer order. audit: true because the owner's order screen subscribes to this table for new
# orders arriving without a reload (Harper refuses subscribe on a table with no audit store).
# Line items are a snapshot of name and price at the time of ordering, so a later price change never
# rewrites an old order.
# customerUserId is the User row of the signed-in customer who placed it, and null for a guest order.
# Indexed: the customer's own order list is that equality plus a sort on placedAt. It is set from the
# session at checkout and never from the request body, and account deletion clears it back to null.
# updatedAt is Harper's: a write that restates a stored row must drop it before putting it back.
type Order @table(audit: true) {
  id: ID @primaryKey
  code: String @indexed
  placedAt: String @indexed
  status: String @indexed
  queue: String @indexed
  fulfilment: String @indexed
  customerUserId: String @indexed
  customerName: String
  customerPhone: String
  deliveryAddress: String
  deliveryPostcode: String
  items: [Any]
  itemsTotalCents: Int
  deliveryFeeCents: Int
  totalCents: Int
  paymentStatus: String @indexed
  paymentRef: String @indexed
  readyEstimate: String
  personalDetailsClearedAt: String @indexed
  updatedAt: Long @updatedTime
}

# A single row, id "store", holding the shop-level settings the owner edits. The resources fall back
# to built-in defaults when the row is absent, so the app works before it is ever saved.
# updatedAt is Harper's. StoreSettingsApi already never sends one, which is the single reason this
# one resource's saves kept working while every other admin save answered 400.
type StoreSetting @table {
  id: ID @primaryKey
  storeName: String
  acceptingOrders: Boolean
  pausedMessage: String
  pickupEnabled: Boolean
  deliveryEnabled: Boolean
  deliveryFeeCents: Int
  deliveryPostcodes: [String]
  pickupEstimateMinutes: Int
  deliveryEstimateMinutes: Int
  updatedAt: Long @updatedTime
}

ownerRule.note: Read-only, available items only. Now also returns photoUrl for an item whose photoUpdatedAt is set — the URL is /MenuPhotoApi/<id>?v=<photoUpdatedAt>, never the bytes.
The shop-level facts a customer needs; nothing private. Unchanged this pass.
Serves one menu item's photo bytes with its stored content type. Read by primary key only — no listing, no search. 404 when the item has no photo.

Public write; guest checkout unchanged. Never trust the basket: every line is re-read from MenuItem and re-priced server-side. New this pass: when the request carries a valid session, customerUserId is stamped from that session — never from the body, which still may not set totals, status, queue, paymentStatus, paymentRef, code or customerUserId.
Reachable only by the order's own random code. One order per request, no listing. Works identically for a guest order and a signed-in customer's order.

A signed-in customer's own orders only: customerUserId equals the session's user id, taken from the session and never from the query. Orders placed as a guest carry null and are reachable by nobody here. Newest first on the indexed placedAt.
Role exactly admin. Deleting an item also deletes its MenuItemPhoto row, so no orphan bytes are left behind. Every write still goes through withoutManaged().

Role exactly admin. POST takes { dataBase64, contentType } for one existing item, refuses anything but image/jpeg or image/png, refuses over 5 MB decoded, verifies the stored bytes read back at the written length and deletes the row if they do not (rule 8), then stamps MenuItem.photoUpdatedAt through withoutManaged(). DELETE removes the photo row and clears photoUpdatedAt.

Role exactly admin, re-read from the User row on every call including the live stream. The only place customer names, phones and addresses are listed. Unchanged this pass except that a listed order may now show it was placed by a signed-in customer.
Role exactly admin. Reads LoopRun for the last-cleared date; never writes it. Unchanged this pass.

routes.notes: The menu by category with a running basket. An item whose photoUrl is present shows the photo beside its name and price, lazily loaded, with a fixed-size frame so the list does not jump; an item with no photoUrl renders exactly as today — no placeholder, no broken image, no request. The header shows 'Sign in' when nobody is signed in and the customer's name linking to /my-orders when somebody is.

Pickup or delivery; name and phone always, address and postcode for delivery. Guest checkout is unchanged and is still the default for anyone not signed in. When signed in, the page prefills name, phone and delivery address from the customer's most recent order (the first row of GET /CustomerOrderApi) and falls back to the account name; every field stays editable and whatever is submitted is what the order stores. The page never sends a user id — the server takes it from the session.
Confirmation by the order's own code. Identical for a guest order and a signed-in customer's order.

The customer's own sign-in page, with two tabs: 'Create an account' (email, password, name optional) and 'Sign in' (email, password). Either one lands them back where they came from — /checkout when they arrived from the basket, otherwise /my-orders. Below both: 'Forgotten your password? Email me a link', which calls request-link with next=/my-orders; the emailed link signs them in and the page they land on offers 'Set a new password'. Shows the server's refusal text plainly — an address already registered, a password that is too short, email not configured, or a refusal from the account limit — rather than a generic failure.

A signed-in customer's own page. Their past orders newest first — order code, date, the items, total and current status, each linking to its confirmation page — and an empty state saying orders placed as a guest before the account existed are not listed. Below the list: set a new password, and delete my account behind a confirmation that says the orders stay in the shop's records with no account attached. Not signed in: a prompt with a link to /sign-in, never a blank page.
Hub: how many orders are waiting, links to the three screens.
The live queue. Unchanged this pass.

Add, edit, hide and remove items; change prices. New: each item's add/edit dialog has a photo control — current photo with Replace and Remove, or 'Choose a photo' when there is none. The chosen file is drawn to a canvas in the browser and re-encoded as JPEG no wider than 1200px before upload, so a phone photo arrives small and the menu stays quick; the 5 MB cap is the server's guard on what is left. The item is saved first, then the photo is uploaded against its id, and a photo failure is reported without losing the saved item. Saving with no photo chosen leaves the item with none.
Pause ordering, pickup/delivery switches, delivery fee, postcode list, time estimates, last-cleared date. Unchanged.

tables.notes: Pizzas, sides and drinks across three categories, whole-cent prices. Two of them (the two pizzas QA will see first) carry photoUpdatedAt so the photo path has data on first load.

Written by scripts/seed.js, not by a YAML file: a Blob seeded from YAML text would store the text rather than an image, so the script generates two small solid-colour PNGs in code and writes them under the matching MenuItem ids with contentType image/png.

A spread across the three queues and both fulfilment kinds. Every line carries {menuItemId, name, priceCents, quantity} so the owner's queue shows a real per-line price. Two of the six carry customerUserId set to the deterministic id of customer1@example.com, so the past-orders page has data; the rest leave it null as guest orders, and one of those belongs to customer2's address as a guest order that must NOT appear in customer1's list.
The single id 'store' row: open for orders, pickup and delivery on, a fee, a short postcode list, both estimates.

accounts.notes: The shop owner. Signs in with the emailed link, or with the admin password in the preview.
A customer account with a password set, and two seeded orders linked to it.
A second customer account with a password set and no linked orders — the one QA uses to prove one customer cannot see another's orders, and that the owner screens refuse a customer.

migrations.note: Additive and nullable. Every existing order keeps null, which is exactly right: they were placed as guests and must not appear in anybody's account (story customer-view-past-orders). Nothing is renamed, nothing is dropped.
Additive and nullable. Every existing item keeps null, meaning no photo, and the menu renders as it does today.
A new table, empty on arrival. Its id is the MenuItem id, so there is nothing to key off and nothing to migrate.

migrationPlan.notes: No rename, no type change, no drop and no hidden field. Adding @indexed to the new Order.customerUserId is a fresh attribute rather than an index over existing data, so there is no INDEX_REBUILDING window on a column anything already reads.

claudeMd: # CLAUDE.md — Pizza Shop Online Ordering ## 1. Product A phone-first ordering site for one pizza shop. Customers browse the menu, build a basket, choose pickup or delivery, give a name and phone number (and an address for delivery), and check out — as a guest, or signed in to a customer account that keeps their order history. The shop owner signs in with a link emailed to their invited address and gets three screens: a live order queue, a menu editor and shop settings. Decided with the owner before the build, and load-bearing: - **Guest checkout is untouched.** Nobody has to make an account to order. A visitor who is not signed in gets exactly the checkout they get today, and the order they place carries no account. - **Customer accounts, email and password.** Anyone may create one (`accessModel.signUp: "open"`). A customer account is role `member`; it changes nothing about who may manage the shop, which is still role exactly `admin` and still only the owner's invited address. A forgotten password is recovered by an emailed link that signs them in, after which they set a new one. - **An account lasts until its customer deletes it.** There is no expiry and no inactivity sweep. Deleting an account removes the `User` row and clears `customerUserId` on that customer's orders, which stay in the shop's records as ordinary orders. - **A menu item may have one photo.** JPEG or PNG, at most 5 MB as stored, shown on the public menu beside the item. The owner may replace or remove it; an item without one looks as it does today. - **Fixed menu.** No sizes, crusts or toppings. **ASAP only**, no scheduling. **Menu prices are final**, no tax line. **Delivery by postcode list**, **one flat delivery fee** the owner sets. - **Payment through the owner's own Stripe account.** Until that key is in place, checkout places the order with `paymentStatus: 'pay_at_store'`. Both paths must keep working. - **Twelve-month retention on an order's personal details**, unchanged, and it applies the same way to a guest order and to a signed-in customer's order. It never touches the account itself. Form factor: phone. One thing per screen, big tap targets, no side-by-side panes. Look: `studio`. ### This pass Three things, and nothing else: customer accounts with email-and-password sign-in; a signed-in customer's order linked to their account and listed on a page of their own; and a photo per menu item, uploaded in the editor and shown on the public menu. Out of scope, and not to be "fixed on the way past": saved cards, loyalty or rewards; editing or cancelling a placed order from the account; attaching a customer's earlier guest orders to a new account; more than one photo per item or any cropping tool; and any change to who may sign in as the shop owner. The two open frontend reports from the last pass — new orders needing a reload on `/manage/orders`, and the 'Estimated ready' wording on the confirmation page — are also still open and still out of scope here. ## 8. Data model Five tables in `schema.graphql`. `User`, `MagicLink`, `EmailLog` and `EmailSuppression` come from the sign-in kit and `StripeEvent` from the payments kit, each in its own `schema.*.graphql` — never redeclare one, and never `@relationship` across files. **This pass is additive only**: two new nullable fields and one new table. Nothing is renamed, retyped or dropped. ### The rule that still governs every write: never write a timestamp Harper owns A field declared `@createdTime` or `@updatedTime` is assigned by Harper in epoch milliseconds. No record this app writes may carry a key for one — not a fresh value, and not the value just read off the stored row. Harper refuses such a write with a bare `400` and no JSON body, which is the whole of the defect that made every menu save and every order-status tap answer "Bad Request". **The trap is the spread, not the literal**: `{ ...existing, status }` names `updatedAt` because the stored row has one. Every writer passes its record through `withoutManaged(record, table)` from `lib/managed-fields.js`, and `managed-fields-probe` holds `MANAGED_FIELDS` equal to the `@createdTime`/`@updatedTime` fields the SDL declares. The fields are `MenuItem.createdAt`, `MenuItem.updatedAt`, `Order.updatedAt` and `StoreSetting.updatedAt`. The new work obeys it in two places that are easy to get wrong: stamping `MenuItem.photoUpdatedAt` after an upload restates a stored MenuItem row, and clearing `Order.customerUserId` during account deletion restates a stored Order row. Both go through `withoutManaged()`. **`MenuItemPhoto` carries no managed field at all** — `uploadedAt` is a plain string the app writes — so replacing a photo cannot reintroduce the fault on a new table. The tables: - **`MenuItem`** — one row per menu item. `priceCents` is whole cents; no floats in money. `category`, `available` and `sortOrder` are indexed because the menu is read as `available == true` sorted by `category` then `sortOrder`. **New: `photoUpdatedAt`**, a plain ISO string the app writes, null when the item has no photo. It is not indexed because nothing filters or sorts by it: it is read off rows the menu already has, and it doubles as the `?v=` cache-buster on the photo URL so a replaced photo is not served from a stale cache. - **`MenuItemPhoto`** — **new**. One row per photographed item, `id` = the `MenuItem` id, so an item has at most one photo by construction and replacing one is a `put` on the same key rather than a uniqueness check Harper cannot make. `data` is a `Blob`: stored outside the record and streamable, which is why the bytes never ride along on a menu listing. Per rule 8 the write is `new Blob([buf], { type })`, never `createBlob`, and it is **verify-on-write** — read the stored blob's size back and delete the row if it does not match what was written, so a half-written photo never leaves a record pointing at nothing. The upload body is base64 in JSON rather than raw bytes: Harper hands a `Resource` a parsed body, and the base64 path needs no raw-body capture. Limits live in one module with the other menu rules: `image/jpeg` or `image/png` only, 5 MB decoded. - **`Order`** — one row per order, `@table(audit: true)`; the audit store is what lets the owner's queue subscribe. `items` is a `[Any]` snapshot of `{menuItemId, name, priceCents, quantity}` taken at checkout, so a later price change never rewrites a placed order and **nothing reads a price back through `menuItemId`** — including anything to do with photos. `code` is 32 random URL-safe characters and is the only key the confirmation page uses. `queue` is derived from `status`, never sent. `paymentStatus`/`paymentRef` as today. **New: `customerUserId`**, the `User` id of the signed-in customer who placed it and null for a guest order. Indexed, because the customer's own list is that equality plus a sort on the indexed `placedAt` — a list page sorting on an unindexed field with no filter beside it is a 404, not a slow query. It is written from the session at checkout and never from a request body, and it is the only new way an order can be reached. - **`StoreSetting`** — exactly one row, id `store`, read by primary key, defaults in code. - **`LoopRun`** — the template's. The nightly retention sweep writes one row per occurrence with the deterministic id `clear-personal-details:YYYY-MM-DD`, claimed before the work is done. Retention is unchanged and is deliberately not extended to accounts: the sweep clears an order's name, phone, address and postcode twelve months after `placedAt` and stamps `personalDetailsClearedAt`, whether or not the order has a `customerUserId`, and it never touches a `User` row. **An account ends only when its customer deletes it.** A cleared order still appears in that customer's history with its code, date, items, total and status — the personal fields are what went, not the order. ## 9. Auth and owner rules `accessModel`: `signIn: "optional"`, **`signUp: "open"`**, `entry: "/"`, `callerAuth: "none"`. The shop is open to anyone; signing in as a customer adds an order history; signing in as the owner is what reaches the management screens. **`signUp` moves from `invited` to `open` this pass, and that is the only change to the front door.** It is set by the deploy from this field (`AUTH_OPEN_SIGNUP`) and by nothing else — no sentence in this file turns it on. Open sign-up creates **`role: 'member'`** rows and nothing more: the owner's seat is still taken only through `ownerMayJoin`/`Bootstrap` or an admin invite, and every management route still demands role exactly `admin`, re-read from the `User` row on every call. Opening sign-up must never be read as opening the owner screens. **There is one sign-in in this app and it is the kit's.** Do not write a second session cookie, a second credential store or a parallel auth resource. What this pass needs that the kit does not yet do is added **inside the kit's own files**, which are this app's files now: - `resources/AuthApi.js` — **`POST /AuthApi/register`** `{ email, password, name? }`: refuses unless `config.auth.openSignup()`, normalizes the address, creates the row through `claimUserForEmail` with `role: ROLE_MEMBER` (so the tier's account quota still applies and its refusal is surfaced verbatim by the page), stores `passwordHash` with the kit's `hashPassword`, and mints the same session cookie the other routes mint. An address that already exists gets one generic refusal that does not distinguish "taken" from "wrong password" on a later attempt. - `resources/AuthApi.js` — **`POST /AuthApi/password`** currently requires `row.role === ROLE_ADMIN`. It now admits any row with a `passwordHash` that is not deactivated. Everything else stays exactly as it is: the same fixed-window counter on `passwordAttemptTimestamps` before the role is looked at, the same PBKDF2 burn for an unknown address, the same single message for every failure (rule 25), and the same 403 — never a 401 (rule 20). - `resources/AccountApi.js` — **`PUT /AccountApi/password`** `{ password }` for the signed-in caller, on their own row only, and **`DELETE /AccountApi/`**, which deletes the caller's own `User` row and first clears `customerUserId` on every order carrying it (indexed equality, `withoutManaged`), so the orders survive as guest orders. Both operate on `loadCaller(this)` and accept no id. **Forgotten passwords reuse the kit's magic link and add no token table.** The customer asks for a link with the existing `POST /AuthApi/request-link`; `MagicLink` already expires in 900 seconds and is keyed by the token hash; redeeming it signs them in exactly as it does for the owner, and they then set a new password with `PUT /AccountApi/password`. No reset-specific token, no second code path. Email goes out through the kit's `lib/email.js` to `api.resend.com`; with no mail key the kit refuses with `email_not_configured` and the page says so plainly. Every resource sets `static loadAsInstance = false` and `target.checkPermission = false` first: this app's people are `User` rows, not Harper roles, so the row rule in the resource **is** the access control. An unauthenticated refusal is a thrown `Response` 403 with `code: 'auth_required'`. | Resource | Rule | |---|---| | `MenuApi` | public, read-only, available items only; returns a photo URL, never photo bytes | | `StoreInfoApi` | public, read-only, shop-level facts; nothing private | | `MenuPhotoApi` | public, read-only, one photo by primary key. No listing and nothing but the image: a photo is as public as the menu it is on | | `CheckoutApi` | public write, guest or signed in. **Never trust the basket**: lines re-read from `MenuItem` and re-priced, fee and postcode rule from `StoreSetting`. The caller may not set totals, `status`, `queue`, `paymentStatus`, `paymentRef`, `code` — **nor `customerUserId`**, which comes from the session or stays null | | `OrderConfirmationApi` | public, reachable only by the order's own random `code`. One order per request, no listing, unchanged for guests | | `CustomerOrderApi` | **owner rule on `customerUserId`** — the session's user id and nothing from the query. A guest order (null) is reachable by nobody here, and one customer can never read another's | | `MenuAdminApi` | admin | | `MenuPhotoAdminApi` | admin | | `StoreSettingsApi` | admin (reads `LoopRun` for the last-cleared date; never writes it) | | `OrderAdminApi` | admin — the only place customer names, phones and addresses are listed | The webhook is the payments kit's `StripeWebhook` and nothing here re-implements it: signature over the raw bytes, idempotent on the Stripe event id, refuses in the preview copy. It sets `paymentStatus`, `status` and `queue` on the order whose `paymentRef` matches, and it must not touch `customerUserId`. Each new owner-scoped surface gets its own suite: `CustomerOrderApi-probe` drives one customer's request and asserts the other customer's order is absent and a guest order is absent, with the negative control being the filter removed; `MenuPhotoAdminApi-probe` asserts the admin refusal, the content-type and size refusals, and — because the stub accepts any field — the **shape of the record handed to `db.MenuItem.put`**, which must name no managed field. ## 10. Pages Phone-first, `studio` look. Ten app routes. `/order/*` is the only wildcard, so `/order` answers too (rule 26). The sign-in kit's own routes (`/login`, `/auth/verify`, `/invite`, `/account`, `/admin/*`) come from `routes/spa.sign-in.json` and must not be repeated in `src/routes.ts`. | Route | Who | What it does | |---|---|---| | `/` | anyone | The menu by category with a running basket; photos beside the items that have one. Entry route | | `/basket` | anyone | Quantities, removals, running total | | `/checkout` | anyone | Pickup or delivery, name and phone, address and postcode for delivery. Guest by default; prefilled from the customer's last order when signed in, and still fully editable | | `/order/:code` | anyone with the link | Confirmation: order number, lines, total, fulfilment, payment state, estimate, status | | `/sign-in` | a customer | **New.** Create an account or sign in with email and password; 'email me a link' for a forgotten password | | `/my-orders` | a signed-in customer | **New.** Their own past orders, newest first; set a new password; delete my account | | `/manage` | owner | Hub: how many orders are waiting, links to the three screens | | `/manage/orders` | owner | The live queue; one tap advances the status | | `/manage/menu` | owner | Add, edit, hide and remove items; change prices; **add, replace or remove a photo** | | `/manage/settings` | owner | Pause ordering, pickup/delivery, fee, postcodes, estimates, last-cleared date | The owner's `/login` stays the owner's: the header's 'Sign in' sends a customer to `/sign-in`, and nothing links a customer to the invite flow. **Photos on the page.** `MenuApi` returns `photoUrl` only for an item whose `photoUpdatedAt` is set, and the menu renders an `` only when it is there — no placeholder element, no request, no broken image for an item without one. The image sits in a fixed-size frame with `loading="lazy"` so the list does not reflow as photos arrive, and an `onError` hides the frame rather than leaving a broken icon. In the editor the chosen file is drawn to a canvas and re-encoded as JPEG no wider than 1200 px before upload, which is browser code and needs no package; the server's 5 MB and content-type checks are the guard behind it, not the mechanism. Every page guards the shape it was handed (`r?.lines ?? []`, `Array.isArray(r?.rows)`) and renders an empty state: the page-boot probe answers `{}` to any GET it has no fixture for, exactly as a half-deployed API would. `/my-orders` must boot for a signed-out visitor and show the prompt, and `createdAt`/`updatedAt` still arrive as epoch-millisecond numbers on rows written since the managed- fields fix and as ISO strings on older ones, so any formatter accepts both.

planCard.summary: Customers can create an account with an email and password and see their past orders, guest checkout stays exactly as it is, and every menu item can carry a photo that shows on the menu.

people.title: Your customers can create an account — or carry on as guests
people.detail: An email address and a password. Anyone can sign up. Ordering without an account works exactly as it does today, and stays the default for anyone not signed in.

people.title: A forgotten password is sorted out by email
people.detail: The customer types their email address, gets a link, taps it, and sets a new password. The same way you get into your own screens.

people.title: Nothing changes about how you get in
people.detail: You still sign in with a link emailed to your invited address, and the management screens are still yours alone. Opening sign-up to customers does not give anyone a way in there.

canDo.title: An order placed while signed in is saved to that customer's account
canDo.detail: The confirmation page and the order in your queue look exactly as they do now.

canDo.title: A customer can look back at their past orders
canDo.detail: Date, order number, the items, the total and the current status. Orders they placed as a guest before signing up are not in the list.

canDo.title: Checkout fills itself in for a signed-in customer
canDo.detail: Name, phone and — for delivery — address come from their last order, and they can change any of it before ordering.

canDo.title: A customer can delete their account whenever they want
canDo.detail: Their account goes; their orders stay in your records as ordinary orders with nobody attached. Accounts last until they are deleted — nothing expires on its own.

canDo.title: You can put a photo on any menu item
canDo.detail: Choose a JPEG or PNG while adding or editing an item, and replace or remove it later. The photo is shrunk in the browser before it is sent, so the menu still loads quickly on a phone.

canDo.title: Photos show on the menu customers see
canDo.detail: Beside the item's name and price. An item with no photo looks exactly as it does today — no gap and no broken picture.

canDo.title: Order details still clear after twelve months
canDo.detail: The name, phone and address on an order are cleared twelve months after it was placed, whether it was a guest order or an account order. That does not touch the customer's account.

screens.title: Create an account or sign in
screens.detail: A new page for customers, with 'forgotten your password' on it.

screens.title: My orders
screens.detail: A customer's own past orders, plus setting a new password and deleting their account.

screens.title: Your menu editor, with photos
screens.detail: Each item gains a photo control: choose, replace or remove.

screens.title: The menu, the basket, checkout and the order queue
screens.detail: All as they are today, with photos on the menu and nothing new to learn.

notInThisVersion.title: Saved cards, loyalty points or rewards
notInThisVersion.detail: An account holds an email, a password, a name and the orders placed with it — nothing else.

notInThisVersion.title: Changing or cancelling an order from a customer's account
notInThisVersion.detail: Past orders are there to look at. Changes still come through you.

notInThisVersion.title: Attaching a customer's earlier guest orders to a new account
